summary: Borges introduced Kafka to the Spanish-speaking world by writing the preface to the 1938 Losada edition of Kafka's stories, published in Buenos Aires. In his 1951 essay "Kafka and His Precursors," he listed Zeno, Browning, and Kierkegaard as Kafka's precursors, then built the argument that a precursor is made not by the earlier writer but by the one who comes later. This is a case where Kafka's reception reshaped Borges's own concept of influence.

In 1969 Borges selected and translated a Spanish edition of selections from Leaves of Grass, publishing it together with his own preface. Earlier, in "Note on Walt Whitman," collected in Other Inquisitions (1952), he had proposed reading the "Walt Whitman" of the poems as a persona invented by the poet — a reading that became the premise of the translation.

Borges translated A Room of One's Own (1936) and Orlando (1937) into Spanish and published both with Editorial Sur in Buenos Aires. These two volumes were among the earliest channels through which Woolf's prose reached Spanish-speaking readers.

Borges translated The Wild Palms into Spanish in 1940, having already published a review of Absalom, Absalom! in a magazine in 1937. His translation became the standard edition through which writers of the Río de la Plata read Faulkner's structuring of time and his use of multiple narrators.

In 1925 Borges translated the final page of Ulysses into Spanish for the magazine Proa and published alongside it the essay "Joyce's Ulysses." It was an introduction that rendered a single page rather than the whole novel, but it was the first place the novel was quoted in Spanish.

In "The Doctrine of Cycles," included in A History of Eternity (1936), Borges examined Nietzsche's eternal recurrence head-on and refuted it. Even so, cyclical time and repeated life remained a premise his later short stories returned to again and again. The form the influence took was repeated refutation, not agreement.

In Discussion (1932), Borges included two essays, "In Defense of Bouvard and Pécuchet" and "Flaubert and His Exemplary Destiny," rereading Flaubert's final novel — widely read as a failure — as a project to gather all knowledge. Borges's recurring motif of a figure who founders while clinging to encyclopedias and lists comes out of this reading.

In his memoir I Confess I Have Lived (1974), Neruda named Whitman as the starting point of his own poetry and wrote that he kept a portrait of him hanging in his study. The way Canto General names America's geology, mining labor, and history of conquest as a catalogue carries the enumerations of Leaves of Grass over into Spanish verse.

Poem 16 of Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair (1924) is an adaptation of a poem from Tagore's The Gardener. After a plagiarism controversy arose in 1934, Neruda added a footnote to later editions disclosing the fact. It is a rare case where the book itself came to record that it was an adaptation.

The two met in Buenos Aires in 1933, and at a PEN Club dinner honoring Rubén Darío they delivered the "al alimón" speech, alternating sentences between them. Neruda included an "Ode to Federico García Lorca" in the Residence on Earth series, and after Lorca's murder in 1936 he responded with Spain in the Heart.

The two met in Paris in the late 1920s and stayed in contact afterward, and during the Spanish Civil War both worked in the same camp supporting the Republic. Neruda recorded his meetings with Vallejo, and Vallejo's death in 1938, directly in his memoir. It was a relationship in which two poets writing in opposite styles in the same language met through politics.

Though they belonged to the same language and almost the same generation, the two writers positioned each other as the opposite pole of their own literature. Borges drew his material from libraries and metaphysical conceits, while Neruda drew his from the continent's geology and politics; there is effectively no record of substantive contact between them, and their remarks about each other were cool. Spanish-language literary history treats the two together as the twentieth century's two opposing axes.

In 1946 Borges published Cortázar's "House Taken Over" in Los Anales de Buenos Aires, the magazine he edited. In a later interview, Cortázar said that what he had learned from Borges was not fantastic subject matter but a discipline of stripping sentences of excess.

On the strength of declining families, narration scattered into fragments, and a disregard for chronological order, scholarship on Latin American fiction repeatedly places Yoknapatawpha and Comala side by side. Rulfo himself, however, denied Faulkner's influence in interviews and said what he had learned came from Nordic writers such as Hamsun and Laxness. This lineage is a scholarly reading, not the author's own endorsement.

In the 1950s, working respectively in the setting of Brazil's sertão and Mexico's Jalisco, the two writers each turned the convention of fiction that documented regional life into language experiment. Comparative literature treats Grande Sertão: Veredas (1956) and Pedro Páramo (1955) together as the two peaks of Latin America's fiction of the interior, but there is no record of contact between the two authors.

For its work of recasting the syntax of the native tongue through neologisms, compound words, and roots drawn from other languages, Brazilian and European criticism has repeatedly placed Grande Sertão: Veredas alongside Ulysses and Finnegans Wake. The basis for this comparison is not any record that Rosa read Joyce, but the overlap in method between the two language experiments.

These are two poles Brazilian prose has reached. Machado undermined the novel's own reliability with a narrator who taunts the reader from a Rio drawing room, while Rosa reassembled the spoken language of the sertão into an artificial idiom, making the sentence itself strange. There is no record of direct contact or lineage between the two; this is a contrast this map draws to show two possibilities of Brazilian fiction side by side.

Between the 1940s and the 1960s, the two writers each bent the idiom of Portuguese prose in a different direction. Rosa layered artificial vocabulary over the spoken language of the sertão, while Lispector twisted syntax to follow inner time. Brazilian literary history treats the two together as two experiments in the same language at the same period, and there is no record of collaboration or a teacher-student relationship between them.

Lispector recalled on several occasions that as a teenager she bought a Portuguese edition of Mansfield's story collection Bliss and Other Stories at a secondhand bookshop and felt that the book was herself. Her early stories, which took as their narrative unit not events but short scenes where a character's consciousness collides with things, use a form that came from Mansfield.

When Near to the Wild Heart appeared in 1943, Brazilian criticism immediately placed the novel alongside Woolf's rendering of consciousness, and that comparison has remained a constant in Lispector scholarship ever since. Lispector herself said she had not read Woolf at the time of her debut — these are two styles of prose that arrived separately at the same problem, not a lineage.

The title and epigraph of the debut novel Near to the Wild Heart come from a passage in Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, but Lispector said she had only heard the passage secondhand from a friend and had not read Joyce at the time. Because that quotation remained on the cover, criticism has continued to treat the two authors together.

The Lost Steps (1953) overlays a journey upriver with a journey back through time, and scholarship on Latin American fiction repeatedly reads this structure within the frame of the "voyage upriver" established by Heart of Darkness. What lies upriver for Carpentier, however, is not horror but the time of origins, and music.

In his 1975 lecture "An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness," Achebe read the novel as a racist text that uses Africa as a backdrop for Europe. His own novel, which narrates an Igbo village through its own internal logic, is that reading put into practice, and the two texts subsequently became the standard pairing in debates over reading back against the canon.

The title and epigraph of Things Fall Apart (1958) come from Yeats's "The Second Coming." Achebe attached that line about the center failing to hold and things falling apart not to the arrival of white men but to fractures already opening within Igbo society before their arrival.

The title and epigraph of No Longer at Ease (1960) come from the closing lines of Eliot's "Journey of the Magi." That line about returning yet no longer being at ease within the old order sums up exactly the situation of the novel's protagonist, who has returned from studying in England.

The two writers answered back to the same text in different forms. Achebe, in a lecture, indicted Heart of Darkness as a racist text; Salih, in a novel that reversed the route from south to north, turned its metaphor back on itself. Postcolonial criticism treats the two together as exemplars of two ways of responding to the canon.

The two writers overlapped as students at the University of Ibadan in the early 1950s, and in June 1962 both attended the "Conference of African Writers of English Expression" at Makerere University, where they discussed the language and scope of African literature in the same room. During the Nigerian civil war, each engaged with politics in a different way.

In the early 1960s Soyinka aimed at Négritude the remark that a tiger does not proclaim its tigritude, and in Myth, Literature and the African World (1976) he formalized that criticism into a theory. Césaire's declaration of Blackness and Soyinka's counterargument — that it should be proven by action rather than proclamation — form one of African literature's long-standing axes of opposition.

Soyinka's Opera Wonyosi (premiered 1977) is an adaptation that transposes Brecht's The Threepenny Opera to the court of a Central African emperor. He carried over directly into the political satire of his own stage Brecht's device of breaking up scenes with song and placing the audience in the position of judge.

In the same period, the two writers each founded a theater company in their own island or city — the Trinidad Theatre Workshop and Ibadan's "1960 Masks" — drawing the performance traditions of carnival and ritual into the stage language of English-language drama. There is no record of either referencing the other; this is a connection this map draws to place two postcolonial theatrical practices side by side.

At the 1962 Makerere conference, Ngũgĩ handed the manuscript of Weep Not, Child to Achebe, who, as the founding editor of the Heinemann African Writers Series, passed it on to the publisher, and it appeared in the series in 1964. Most of Ngũgĩ's early work after that came out in the same series.

In "The African Writer and the English Language" (1965), Achebe declared he would bend English to carry the weight of Africa, while in Decolonising the Mind (1986), Ngũgĩ announced he would stop writing in English and move to Gikuyu. These two texts, answering the same question in opposite ways, define African literature's debate over language.

Ngũgĩ read Conrad intensively during his time at Leeds University, and A Grain of Wheat (1967), written in that period, transposes the structure of Under Western Eyes — a traitor's confession retraced through multiple viewpoints — to the eve of Kenyan independence. Ngũgĩ himself has acknowledged this debt in essays and interviews.

The two writers both attended the 1962 Makerere conference and debated the conference's very premise — "African writers of English expression" — before later arriving at different conclusions on the question of language. Soyinka kept English but brought in Yoruba time, while Ngũgĩ changed his medium to Gikuyu.

Season of Migration to the North (1966) reverses the route of Heart of Darkness, placing in the conqueror's position not a European entering the darkness but a Sudanese youth entering London. Even the frame-narrator structure that belatedly reconstructs another person's life is taken from Conrad and rewritten in reverse, and postcolonial criticism treats it as the standard example of writing back.

The standard account in the history of the modern Arabic novel holds that only after Mahfouz established the Arabic novel as a settled form in the 1940s and '50s could Salih's generation take that form as a given and experiment with it. In place of the urban chronicle Mahfouz had established, Salih chose a frame narrative and time running in reverse.

For its structure, in which the Cairo Trilogy passes the time of a city and a nation through three generations of one family, scholarship on the Arabic novel repeatedly explains it as a case of the European family-chronicle novel in the line of Buddenbrooks carried over into Arabic. Mahfouz himself also named his reading of the European novel as a condition of his own formation.

Scholarship on the Arabic novel explains the phase after the 1960s, when Mahfouz abandoned realism and moved toward interior monologue and montages of short scenes, as an absorption of post-Joycean European modernist narration. His record of writing the same Cairo twice, in two different ways, is the trace of that absorption.

Carpentier's The Kingdom of This World (1949) and Césaire's play The Tragedy of King Christophe (1963) each treat, in fiction and on stage respectively, the same material — the Haitian Revolution and Henri Christophe, a slave who became king. Caribbean literary studies read the two works together as two ways of turning revolution into narrative.

In 1930s Paris, the two writers, in Spanish and French respectively, wrote poetry that attached the idiom created by the European avant-garde to the body of the colony and the periphery. Their ways of breaking syntax and their political conclusions are close, but there is no record that the two ever met; this map places two trajectories through the same city side by side.

In "The Muse of History" (1974), Walcott rejected both a literature of resentment against colonial rule and a literature of nostalgia for a lost Africa, placing the Caribbean poet instead in the position of Adam, naming things for the first time. The narrative of recovery Césaire built through Négritude, and Walcott's rejection of it, are the two directions of Caribbean poetry.

Walcott's early poetry began by applying, directly, the formal English meter refined by Yeats's generation to Caribbean landscape and figures, and he called Irish writers colonials who had inherited a great language, laying his own situation over theirs. Scholarship on Anglophone poetry repeatedly treats this lineage.

In Canto General (1950) and Omeros (1990) respectively, the two poets placed the landscape and labor of the Americas within the form of the European epic. One catalogued the continent's geology and history of conquest by name; the other attached Homeric names to the fishermen of a single island. There is no record of direct contact; this is a comparison this map draws across the hemisphere.

The two writers each invented a single fictional village — Comala and Wad Hamid respectively — and returned to it across a small handful of books, and both ended their creative careers in an early silence. There is no record of direct contact; the basis for this connection is that the same method of writing one village as an entire world appeared independently on different continents.

Rosa drew the orality of the sertão, and Soyinka the songs and invocations of Yoruba ritual, into their respective written forms. One remade the vocabulary of the novel's sentences; the other restructured the time of the stage. There is no record that either read the other; this connection is placed here to compare two cases that took oral tradition as a founding principle for a written form.
